input.explainer: The pipeline starts from two accessibility trees: a structured text snapshot of the page before the interaction and another of the page after it. Each line describes one on-screen element — its role (button, link, menu, and so on) and its visible text — so the whole screen is captured as readable text rather than pixels.

diff.explainer: The before and after trees are compared line by line to find what the interaction actually changed. Added lines are elements that appeared, deleted lines are elements that went away, and the counts summarize how big the change was. If nothing changed, the interaction told us nothing about the element and the sample stops here.

reject.reasoning: The click revealed a dedicated filter panel with concrete filter controls, a clear and informative change that directly reflects the button's purpose.
reject.explainer: A language model scores whether the observed change is informative enough to describe the element's purpose. Trivial or noisy changes score low and the sample is rejected; a clear, meaningful change is kept and moves on to annotation. This filter keeps low-quality samples out of the dataset.

annotate.functionality: Opens the filter panel so results can be narrowed by attributes such as sale status and stock availability.
annotate.reasoning: After the click, a 'Filter panel' region appeared containing 'On sale' and 'In stock' checkboxes, which were not present before, indicating the button toggles a filtering interface.
annotate.explainer: A language model reads the change and writes a short, high-level description of what the interacted element does — for example, 'opens the options menu'. It works either from the line-by-line diff (manipulation mode) or from a description of the whole page when the interaction navigated somewhere new (describe mode).

verify.reasoning: Given the proposed functionality, the verifier consistently pointed back to the 'Filters' button that was actually clicked across every trial.
verify.explainer: To guard against hallucinated descriptions, a second language-model pass checks consistency: given the proposed functionality, could it point back to the element that was actually clicked? Each check is scored, and only a full-confidence agreement marks the description as consistent. Anything less is flagged as inconsistent.

result.functionality: Opens the filter panel so results can be narrowed by attributes such as sale status and stock availability.
result.explainer: The final outcome for this sample: the functionality description the pipeline settled on (when it produced one), alongside the dataset's ground-truth label when one exists, so a reader can compare the two. The top-level verdict records where the sample ended up — kept, rejected, unchanged, uncheckable, or inconsistent.
